unit.title: Acquire foundation knowledge of massage therapy

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which is the best description of massage?
options: A treatment done only with electrical machines
A medical treatment that cures most illnesses
Using the hands on skin and muscles in set ways
Stretching exercises that the client does alone

questions.stem: Which is a physical effect of massage on the body?
options: Blood flow to the area increases
Body fat melts away from the area
Bones in the area grow stronger
Infections in the area are cured

questions.stem: Which is an effect of a slow, rhythmic massage on the mind?
options: The client feels more alert and anxious
The client's memory gets much better
The client is ready for a heavy workout
The client feels calm and less stressed

questions.stem: What is effleurage?
options: Quick striking with the sides of the hands
Long, smooth stroking with the whole hand
Deep kneading and squeezing of muscle
Small circles with the thumb on one spot

questions.stem: Why is effleurage used at the start and end of a massage, and between other movements?
options: To spread the oil, warm up and link strokes
To break down hard knots deep in the muscle
To wake up the client with brisk tapping
To press on energy points along the spine

questions.stem: Which is a benefit of massage for the skin?
options: It removes all scars and stretch marks
It stops the skin from ever ageing
Dead skin cells are loosened and shed
It makes the skin produce no more oil

questions.stem: Which describes tapotement?
options: Slow, deep strokes towards the heart only
Quick, light striking, such as hacking
Kneading the muscle like dough
Holding still with gentle pressure

questions.stem: Where should tapotement never be used?
options: On large, well-padded muscles
On the thighs of a sports client
On the fleshy part of the shoulders
Over bony areas or the kidney area

questions.stem: Which describes friction movements?
options: Long, light strokes over the whole back
Quick slapping with cupped hands
Gentle rocking of the whole body
Small, deep circles with the thumbs

questions.stem: Which describes vibration?
options: A fine shaking or trembling of the hands
Firm squeezing and rolling of the muscle
Lifting the skin and rolling it between fingers
Brisk hacking with the edge of the hands

questions.stem: On the arms and legs, in which direction are effleurage strokes usually firmest?
options: Away from the heart, towards the hands and feet
Across the limb, from one side to the other
Towards the heart, to help blood in the veins
In small circles on one spot only

questions.stem: How should you decide how much pressure to use?
options: Always press as hard as you can
Ask the client, and never cause pain
Use the same pressure on every client
Press harder each time the client winces

questions.stem: Which of these means you must not give a massage at all that day?
options: The client has a fever or high temperature
The client has a small bruise on one arm
The client had a large meal two days ago
The client has slightly dry skin on the legs

questions.stem: A client has a blood clot in a deep vein of her leg. Why must you not massage her?
options: Massage would make the leg cold
The clot would make your hands sore
The oil would stain the skin over it
The clot could move to the lungs

questions.stem: A client has a small cut on one shoulder. What should you do?
options: Cancel the whole massage and send her home
Avoid that area and massage the rest
Massage over it firmly to help it heal
Rub oil into the cut to clean it

questions.stem: How should you treat an area with varicose veins?
options: Use firm tapotement to break them up
Use deep friction to smooth them out
Avoid them and do not press over them
Massage them hard to push the blood up

questions.stem: A client has a heart condition. What should you do before a massage?
options: Give her a shorter, firmer massage instead
Massage only her back, and not her legs
Use tapotement to help her heart
Ask her to get her doctor's approval

questions.stem: A client tells you she is pregnant. What should you do?
options: Check the Centre's rules and get medical approval
Give a normal full-body massage, lying face down
Use extra-deep pressure on her lower back
Ask her not to tell her doctor about it

questions.stem: A client arrives for a massage after drinking alcohol. What should you do?
options: Give the massage, as it will help sober her up
Give a longer massage so that she can rest
Do not treat her today, and rebook kindly
Give her a strong coffee and then begin

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the consultation before a massage?
options: To sell the client as many products as you can
To check health, needs and contraindications
To find out where the client lives and works
To decide how long your lunch break can be

questions.stem: What is informed consent?
options: The client pays for the whole treatment in advance
The client understands the treatment and agrees
The therapist agrees to treat the client
The client's friend signs the form for her

questions.stem: Part-way through the massage, the client asks you to stop. What should you do?
options: Finish the movement you are doing, then stop
Carry on, as she agreed at the start
Persuade her to let you finish the back
Stop at once and ask if she is all right

questions.stem: A 15-year-old asks for a massage. What must you have before treating her?
options: Consent from her parent or guardian
A note from one of her school friends
Payment in cash before she lies down
A signed letter from her teacher

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of draping (covering the client with towels)?
options: To keep the oil off the couch cover
To make the treatment room look tidy
To keep the client warm and private
To stop the client from moving about

questions.stem: Which is correct draping practice?
options: Uncover only the area being worked on
Uncover the whole body so you can see
Use one small hand towel for the body
Let the towel slip so you can work faster

questions.stem: How should the client get ready for a back massage?
options: Undress while the therapist watches to help
Undress fully in the reception area
Stay fully dressed in a thick sweater
Undress in private, then lie under a towel

questions.stem: Which shows a professional manner during a massage?
options: Talking about your own problems at great length
Telling the client about other clients
Speaking calmly and keeping to the treatment
Taking phone calls while you work

questions.stem: Which is the right appearance for a massage therapist?
options: Long painted nails and lots of bracelets
Short, clean nails and hair tied back
Strong perfume and loose, long hair
Rings on each hand and a long scarf

questions.stem: How should client record cards be kept?
options: On the reception desk where anyone can read them
Locked away, shown only to staff who need them
Pinned on the staff noticeboard for all to see
Taken home by the therapist to read at night

questions.stem: A client asks you what is wrong with her painful knee. What should you say?
options: Tell her she has arthritis and what to take
Say it is a torn muscle and massage it hard
Tell her it is nothing and to ignore it
Say you cannot diagnose; suggest a doctor

questions.stem: When should a massage therapist wash her hands?
options: Before and after every client
Only at the end of the working day
Only if her hands look dirty or oily
Only after she has used the toilet

questions.stem: How often should towels and couch roll be changed?
options: Once a day, after the last client
Once a week, unless they look dirty
Fresh ones for every single client
Only when a client complains

questions.stem: Before using sweet almond oil, what must you check?
options: That the oil is warm from the sun
That the client likes the smell of it
That the bottle is nearly full
That the client has no nut allergy

questions.stem: How should massage oil be used?
options: Pour a large pool of it straight onto the back
Warm a little in your hands, then add more
Use as much as possible so it soaks in
Spray it onto the client's face first

questions.stem: How can you stop massage oil from becoming contaminated?
options: Use a pump bottle, or pour some into a bowl
Dip your oily hands back into the main bottle
Leave the bottle open so it can breathe
Top it up with oil left over from clients

questions.stem: Which room is best for a relaxing massage?
options: Cold, bright and close to the street
Hot, noisy and shared with the nail desk
Warm, quiet, clean and with privacy
Busy, with staff walking through it

questions.stem: Why should the couch be set at the right height for the therapist?
options: So the client can climb onto it more quickly
So that the couch takes up less space in the room
So the therapist can work with a straight back
So the oil does not drip onto the floor

questions.stem: Which posture helps a therapist avoid back injury?
options: Feet together and bent over from the waist
Standing on tiptoe to reach the far side
Arms straight and locked, pushing hard
Feet apart, knees soft, using body weight

questions.stem: When the client lies face down, where is a rolled towel or support usually placed?
options: Under the stomach
Under the ankles
Under the back of the neck
Under the elbows

questions.stem: When the client lies face up, where is a support usually placed to ease the lower back?
options: Under the knees
Under the heels
Under the hips
Under the lower ribs

questions.stem: A client feels light-headed when the massage ends. What should you do?
options: Tell her to stand up quickly and walk it off
Leave her alone in the room to sleep
Help her sit up slowly and give her water
Give her a strong cup of coffee straight away

questions.stem: Which aftercare advice is usually given after a massage?
options: Drink water, rest, and avoid alcohol
Go straight to the gym for a hard workout
Eat a very large, heavy meal straight away
Take a very hot bath as soon as you get home

questions.stem: Which muscle forms the calf at the back of the lower leg?
options: Quadriceps femoris
The gastrocnemius
Biceps brachii
Gluteus maximus

questions.stem: Where are large groups of lymph nodes found?
options: In the fingertips and toes
In the scalp and the ears
Along the shin bones
In the armpits, groin and neck

questions.stem: What should be written on the record card after the massage?
options: The client's opinion of the other staff members
Only the price that the client paid
Areas treated, oil used and any reaction
What the client wore to the salon

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the group of massage movements that knead and squeeze the muscles, such as wringing and picking up?
What is the word for the position in which the client lies face down?
What do the letters DVT stand for?
What is the name of the large muscle of the upper back and the back of the neck?
What is the name of the muscle that covers the shoulder joint and lifts the arm?
What name is given to an unwanted reaction during or after a treatment, such as feeling dizzy?
What is the medical name for the shoulder blade?
What is the medical name for the column of bones that runs down the middle of the back?
Which body system carries lymph and helps the body fight infection?
What is the word for the oil, cream or powder that helps the hands glide during a massage?
Which style of massage, named after a country in northern Europe, uses the classic stroking, kneading and striking movements?
What is the name of the padded rest with a hole that supports the face when the client lies face down?
Which body system is made up of the brain, the spinal cord and the nerves?
What is the name of the large, flat muscle on each side of the middle and lower back?
What is the name of the outer layer of the skin?

essays.stem: Explain what a contraindication to massage is. Give examples of conditions that stop the massage, conditions where one area is avoided, and conditions that need a doctor's approval.
essays.modelAnswer: A contraindication is a condition that means the massage must not go ahead, or must be changed, because it could harm the client or spread infection. Some conditions stop the massage completely, such as a fever or high temperature, an infectious illness or skin infection, being under the influence of alcohol or drugs, a recent operation, or a blood clot in a deep vein. Some conditions mean that only one area is avoided while the rest can be massaged, such as a bruise, a cut or open wound, a recent scar, sunburn, swelling, a recent sprain, or varicose veins. Some conditions need the client's doctor to approve the massage first, such as a heart condition, high or low blood pressure, diabetes, epilepsy, cancer, pregnancy, or taking certain medicines. If I find a contraindication, I explain tactfully without diagnosing, record it, and refer the client to her doctor when needed.
markingPoints: Defines a contraindication: the treatment must not go ahead, or must be changed
Stops the massage: fever, infection, alcohol or drugs, recent operation, blood clot
Area avoided: bruise, cut, recent scar, sunburn, swelling, varicose veins
Needs a doctor's approval: heart condition, blood pressure, diabetes, epilepsy, cancer, pregnancy
Explains tactfully, does not diagnose, records it and refers

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out a consultation and get informed consent before a massage.
essays.modelAnswer: I greet the client and take her to a private area so that she can speak freely. I explain what the massage involves, how long it takes, which areas I will work on, what she will need to take off and how she will be covered with towels. I ask about her health, her medicines, any allergies (including nut allergies, because of some oils), recent injuries or operations, and what she hopes to get from the massage. I check for contraindications and agree the pressure and the areas with her. I make sure she understands and agrees: this is informed consent. She signs the consultation form, and if she is under 18, a parent or guardian must sign too. I tell her that she can ask me to stop or change anything at any time. I keep the form private and locked away.
markingPoints: Private area; explains the treatment, the areas, undressing and towels
Asks about health, medicines, allergies and her goals
Checks for contraindications and agrees the areas and pressure
Informed consent: the client understands and agrees, and signs the form (a parent or guardian if under 18)
Tells the client she can stop at any time; keeps the records confidential

essays.stem: Describe how you would drape a client for a back massage, and explain why draping matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the client undresses, I explain what to take off and how to lie on the couch under the towel. I leave the room while she undresses and gets onto the couch face down under a large towel, and I knock before coming back in. I check that she is comfortable, with a support under her ankles. For the back massage, I fold the towel down to her waist and tuck it in firmly so that it will not slip. I cover her legs with a second towel to keep her warm. Only the back is uncovered, and private areas always stay covered. When I move to another area, I cover the back first, then uncover the next area. Draping matters because it protects the client's privacy and dignity, keeps her warm and relaxed, shows a professional manner, and protects both the client and the therapist.
markingPoints: Explains first, and leaves the room while the client undresses and gets under the towel
Client positioned comfortably, with supports
Only the back uncovered; towel tucked in securely; private areas always covered
Covers one area before uncovering the next; an extra towel for warmth
Reasons: privacy and dignity, warmth and relaxation, a professional manner and protection

essays.stem: Explain what is meant by a professional manner for a massage therapist, giving examples.
essays.modelAnswer: A professional manner means behaving in a way that makes clients feel safe, respected and confident in the therapist. It starts with appearance: a clean uniform, short, clean nails without polish, hair tied back, no jewellery on the hands and wrists, and fresh breath. The therapist is on time, greets the client politely and explains the treatment clearly. She speaks in a calm, quiet voice and keeps the talk on the client and the treatment, not on her own problems or gossip about others. She respects boundaries: she drapes the client properly, touches only the areas agreed at the consultation, never makes personal or sexual comments, and stops if the client asks. She keeps client information confidential and stays within her training, so she does not diagnose but refers to a doctor. She keeps the room clean and tidy and records every treatment.
markingPoints: Clean, neat appearance: uniform, short nails, hair tied back, no jewellery
On time and polite, with clear explanations and a calm voice
Keeps the talk on the client and treatment; no gossip or personal problems
Respects boundaries: draping, agreed areas only, no improper comments, stops when asked
Confidentiality, and working within her training (no diagnosis; refers)

essays.stem: Describe the five classic groups of massage movements and the main effect of each.
essays.modelAnswer: Effleurage is long, smooth stroking with the whole hand. It is used to start and finish, to spread the oil and to link the other movements. It warms the area, helps blood and lymph flow, and relaxes the client. Petrissage is kneading, wringing, picking up and rolling the muscles. It is deeper, loosens tight muscles and helps waste to be carried away. Tapotement is quick, light, rhythmic striking, such as hacking and cupping. It stimulates and wakes up the area and tones the skin, and it is used only on well-padded areas, never over bones or the kidneys. Friction is small, deep, circular movements with the thumbs or fingertips on one spot. It helps loosen tight knots and stiff areas. Vibration is a fine shaking or trembling of the hands or fingertips. It can stimulate the nerves or, when gentle, soothe the client. The therapist chooses and mixes the movements to suit each client.
markingPoints: Effleurage: long stroking; starts, links and ends; warms and relaxes
Petrissage: kneading, wringing and picking up; loosens muscles
Tapotement: quick striking (hacking, cupping); stimulates; not over bones
Friction: small, deep circles on one spot; loosens knots
Vibration: fine shaking; stimulates or soothes

essays.stem: Explain the effects of massage on the skin, the muscles, the circulation and the mind.
essays.modelAnswer: On the skin, massage loosens and removes dead skin cells and brings more blood to the surface, so the skin looks healthy and feels warm; with oil, it is left softer. On the muscles, massage warms and relaxes tight muscles, eases stiffness and tension, and can help a tired muscle recover. On the circulation, strokes towards the heart help the blood in the veins to return, so more oxygen and food reach the tissues. Massage also helps the lymph to move, which carries waste away and can reduce puffiness. On the mind, slow, rhythmic movements calm the nerves, reduce stress and worry, and help the client sleep and feel better in herself. Brisk movements, such as tapotement, have the opposite effect and can wake the client up. These effects help the client, but massage does not cure illness, and a therapist should not claim that it does.
markingPoints: Skin: removes dead cells, brings blood to the surface, leaves it softer
Muscles: warms, relaxes, eases stiffness and tension
Circulation: helps blood return to the heart, so more oxygen and food reach the tissues
Lymph: helps carry waste away and reduce puffiness
Mind: calms, reduces stress and helps sleep (brisk movements stimulate)

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare the treatment room and the couch before a client arrives for a massage.
essays.modelAnswer: I check that the room is clean, tidy and private, with a door that closes and a sign so that no one walks in. The room should be warm enough for a client who is partly undressed, well ventilated and quiet, with soft lighting and calm music if the client wants it. I check that the couch is stable, with the legs locked, and set at the right height for me. I wipe it with disinfectant and cover it with fresh couch roll, then lay out clean towels for draping, supports for the ankles or knees, and a gown if needed. I put the oil or cream in a pump bottle or a clean bowl, with tissues, a bin with a lid and the consultation form ready. I make sure there is a chair, a hook for clothes and drinking water. Finally, I wash my hands and check my own appearance.
markingPoints: Room clean, private, warm, quiet and ventilated, with soft light
Couch checked as stable, set at the right height, disinfected, with fresh couch roll
Fresh towels, supports and a gown laid out
Oil in a pump bottle or clean bowl; tissues, a lidded bin and forms ready
Chair, clothes hook and water; therapist washes hands and checks her appearance

essays.stem: Explain how a massage therapist should stand and move to avoid injury, and why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: The therapist sets the couch at the right height, so that she can work with a straight back and does not have to bend over. She stands with her feet apart, one in front of the other, and keeps her knees soft, so that she can move her weight from one foot to the other. She uses her body weight, leaning from the legs, to give pressure, rather than pushing only with her arms and thumbs. She keeps her shoulders relaxed and her wrists as straight as she can, and she walks around the couch instead of stretching to reach the far side. She takes short breaks, stretches her hands and wrists between clients, and does not book too many massages in a row. This matters because massage is hard physical work. Poor posture can cause back, neck, wrist and thumb injuries that could stop her working, and a relaxed therapist also gives a smoother massage.
markingPoints: Couch at the right height; straight back, no bending over
Feet apart, knees soft, weight moved between the legs
Uses body weight, not just arm and thumb strength; relaxed shoulders and straight wrists
Walks around the couch instead of stretching; takes breaks and stretches the hands
Says why: avoids back, neck, wrist and thumb injuries, and gives a better massage

essays.stem: Describe the hygiene steps a therapist takes before, during and after a massage.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the massage, the therapist wears a clean uniform, keeps her nails short and covers any cut on her hands with a waterproof plaster. She wipes the couch and trolley with disinfectant, puts down fresh couch roll and lays out fresh towels for this client only. She washes her hands with soap and water, or uses hand sanitiser, in front of the client. She checks the client for skin infections or open wounds. During the massage, she takes the oil from a pump bottle or a clean bowl, so that the main bottle is not contaminated, and she does not touch her own face or hair. If she has to stop, she washes her hands again before carrying on. After the massage, she washes her hands, puts used towels in the laundry bin and couch roll in a lidded bin, cleans the couch and the bowl, and has the towels washed hot, as the Centre's rules say.
markingPoints: Clean uniform, short nails, cuts covered
Couch disinfected; fresh couch roll and towels for each client
Hands washed before and after; client checked for infection
Oil taken from a pump or a clean bowl so the stock is not contaminated
After: laundry and waste dealt with, and the couch and equipment cleaned

essays.stem: Describe the aftercare advice you would give after a massage, the unwanted reactions a client may have, and what you would do about them.
essays.modelAnswer: After the massage, I let the client rest for a few minutes and help her sit up slowly. I advise her to drink water, rest for the rest of the day if she can, and avoid alcohol, a heavy meal and hard exercise for a few hours. If oil was used, she can leave it to soak in, or take a warm (not very hot) shower later. Some clients have unwanted reactions. She may feel light-headed or dizzy when she sits up, so I help her sit up slowly, give her water and do not let her stand until she feels well. She may feel tired, have a mild headache, need to pass water more often, feel emotional, or have a little muscle soreness the next day; these usually pass within a day. If she has redness or itching from the oil, I remove the oil and record it. I write any reaction and the advice I gave on her record card, and suggest she sees a doctor if anything does not settle.
markingPoints: Rest, then sit up slowly
Drink water; avoid alcohol, a heavy meal and hard exercise for a while
Names reactions: light-headedness, tiredness, headache, soreness, needing the toilet, feeling emotional
Correct action: sit up slowly, give water, stay until well; remove the oil for a skin reaction
Records reactions and advice; refers to a doctor if a reaction does not settle

practical1.title: Consultation, consent and draping for a back massage (role play with client cards)
practical1.brief: Work as a group of 4 or 5 in the Centre's treatment room. As a group, prepare the room and the couch for a massage. The assessor gives each member a made-up client card; no real health details are used, and some cards include a contraindication. Each member, in turn, plays the therapist and carries out a full consultation with another member, who plays the client from the card. The therapist explains the treatment, checks for contraindications, decides whether to treat, avoid an area or refer to a doctor, and completes the consultation form, which the 'client' signs. The therapist then shows correct draping for a back massage and for the front of the legs, with the 'client' lying on the couch fully clothed, so that draping is practised over clothing. The other members watch and fill in a peer-check sheet for each therapist. Photograph each stage below, showing only the couch, towels, forms and hands, never faces. Hand in once for the whole group, with the forms and check sheets.
materials: A massage couch with a face cradle, couch roll and a step if needed
Large and small towels, ankle and knee supports, and a gown
A trolley with massage oil in a pump bottle, a clean bowl and tissues
Made-up client cards from the assessor
Consultation forms, peer-check sheets and pens
Disinfectant, paper towels, a lidded bin and a laundry bin
photos: The treatment room and couch set up and ready
Each member's completed consultation form (made-up details only)
The decision for each card (treat, avoid an area, or refer), written on the form
Draping for a back massage: only the back area uncovered, the towel tucked in
Draping for the front of the legs, with a support under the knees
The room cleaned, with the towels in the laundry bin
checklist: Helped prepare a clean, warm, private room and a safe, correctly set couch
Explained the treatment clearly and politely, in a calm voice
Asked about health, medicines, allergies and goals, and checked for contraindications
Made the right decision for the card (treat, avoid an area, or refer to a doctor)
Got informed consent, and completed the form with the client's signature
Draped correctly: only the area to be worked uncovered, towels secure, private areas covered
Kept a professional manner and kept the client's information confidential
Helped clean and tidy the room afterwards
safety: Practise draping over clothing only; no one undresses for this task
Use only made-up client details; do not write down real health information
Check that the couch is stable and its legs are locked before anyone gets on
Help the 'client' on and off the couch, using the step if needed
Follow the Centre's rules on privacy and photographs

practical2.title: The five classic massage movements on a partner's back or forearm
practical2.brief: Work as a group of 4 or 5 in the Centre's treatment room. Each member gives a short massage, of about 15 minutes, to a group partner who agrees, using all five groups of classic movements: effleurage, petrissage, tapotement, friction and vibration. Before starting, the therapist does a quick consultation and contraindication check, asks about nut and other allergies, and gets the partner's consent. The partner chooses either to have the back massaged, lying face down with only the back uncovered and draped with towels, or to stay dressed and have the forearm and hand massaged instead. Members take turns as therapist, client, timekeeper and photographer, so that everyone does each job. The group then makes a labelled photo sheet showing each of the five movements, with one line on what each one does. Photograph only the area being worked and the therapist's hands, never faces. Hand in once for the whole group, with the photo sheet and the record cards.
materials: A massage couch with a face cradle and fresh couch roll
Large and small towels for draping, and ankle supports
A massage oil or cream with the maker's label, in a pump bottle, and a clean bowl
A nut-free, unscented option for anyone with an allergy, or a towel to massage over
Tissues, a timer, consultation and record cards, and pens
Disinfectant, paper towels, a lidded bin and a laundry bin
Paper or card for the photo sheet
photos: The room and couch set up, with the oil in a pump bottle or bowl
The partner draped, with only the area to be worked uncovered
checklist: Did a quick consultation, checked allergies and contraindications, and got consent
Prepared the area, washed hands, and used the oil hygienically
Draped correctly and kept the partner warm and covered
Performed effleurage, petrissage, tapotement, friction and vibration correctly
Kept the movements smooth and rhythmic, with a pressure checked with the partner
Kept tapotement off the spine, bones and the kidney area
Kept a good working posture throughout
Gave aftercare advice, completed the record card and cleaned the area
safety: Do not massage any member who has a contraindication; tell the assessor
Ask about nut and other allergies before using any oil or cream
No tapotement over bones, the spine or the kidney area
Stop at once if the partner feels pain or dizziness, or asks you to stop
Help the partner sit up and get off the couch slowly
Follow the Centre's rules on privacy, consent and photographs
